situation:
You are the human resources manager at ALDERGROVE TOOLWORKS, a regional manufacturer of hydraulic fittings and couplings that runs three plants. The vice president of operations (judge) has asked you to bring a recommendation to a meeting this afternoon about a position it created last spring and never defined.

ALDERGROVE TOOLWORKS has supplied the same equipment builders for close to thirty years and is the largest employer in two of its towns. For the past two years a new entrant has been taking those builders' smaller orders at prices the company cannot match. In answer, ALDERGROVE TOOLWORKS put a plant account representative at each of the three plants, a role no one here had held before.

The representatives sell to independent repair shops, almost entirely by email. No one wrote work rules for the position, so each plant has improvised its own. One representative mails everyone on contact lists bought from a trade directory; another mails only shops that asked to hear from the company. Nothing done so far breaks the law and no customer has objected, but the three plants answer the same question differently.

The vice president of operations (judge) wants you to analyze the choice and recommend one course. Building the onboarding program — written work rules, ethics training, and one standard for how representatives may collect and use customer email addresses — would take six months and the money already committed to replacing a press at the oldest plant, and it earns that money back only if the sales forecast behind the role holds. Leaving the representatives to sell and writing rules once the year's orders are counted keeps the press on schedule and leaves three plants improvising through the season the company is trying to win back.

You will present your recommendation to the vice president of operations (judge) in a meeting to take place in his/her office. The vice president of operations (judge) will begin the meeting by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented and have answered the vice president's (judge) questions, the vice president of operations (judge) will thank you for your work.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the vice president of operations (judge) at ALDERGROVE TOOLWORKS. Business background is the same as the situation above. You created the plant account representative position to hold the smaller accounts a new entrant has been taking, and you have since learned that the three plants are running the position three different ways because nobody ever wrote rules for it.

You want the human resources manager to analyze the choice and recommend whether to build the onboarding program now or wait until the year's orders are counted, and to tell you plainly what the recommendation costs.

During the presentation you are to ask the following questions of the participant:
judgeQuestions: If we start the program, what happens in a representative's first week?
Who at each plant would run it, and what would you have them do first?
